title: How would you estimate how many hairdressers work in London?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How many hairdressers work in London?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: About 26,000 full-time hairdressers and barbers work in London, which means 30,000 to 35,000 people once you allow for part-time work. You get there by sizing demand (how many haircuts Londoners need in a year) and dividing by supply (how many one hairdresser can do). Try your own estimate before you read on.
body:
The question

How many hairdressers work in London?

This is a classic demand-meets-capacity question, the same family as the piano tuners puzzle. You cannot count hairdressers directly, so you count the work they do and divide by how much work one person can handle.

Clarify before you calculate

  • Are barbers included? Usually yes. Ask, because men's cuts are a large share of visits.
  • People or full-time equivalents? Many hairdressers work part time. The demand-and-capacity method gives full-time equivalents (FTEs); you convert to headcount at the end.
  • Who counts as a customer? London residents. Commuters getting a cut near the office roughly cancel out Londoners who get theirs elsewhere.

Rough guess: "Tens of thousands. There are salons and barbers on almost every high street."

Step by step

1. Demand: haircuts needed a year

  • Men and boys, about 4.5M, visit roughly every seven weeks: about 7 visits a year → 4.5M × 7 = 31.5M.
  • Women and girls, about 4.5M, visit less often but for longer: about 5 visits a year → 4.5M × 5 = 22.5M.
  • Total: 54M visits a year, an average of 6 per Londoner.

2. Supply: visits one hairdresser can handle

8 clients a day × 5.5 days a week × 48 working weeks = 2,112 visits a year.

3. Divide

54M ÷ 2,112 = about 25,600 FTE hairdressers. Round to 26,000.

4. Convert to people

If the average hairdresser works 75% of full-time hours, the headcount is 25,600 ÷ 0.75 = about 34,000 people.

Sanity check from a second angle

Count the shops instead. Walk down a typical London high street and you pass several salons and barbers. Assume about one for every 1,000 residents: 9M ÷ 1,000 = 9,000 shops. At an average of three chairs in use, that is 27,000 hairdressers. That is within about 5% of the demand-side answer.

A third check uses chair time rather than visits, because a men's cut and a colour appointment are very different jobs. Say a men's visit takes 30 minutes and a women's visit 75 minutes on average:

  • 31.5M × 0.5 hours + 22.5M × 1.25 hours = 15.75M + 28.1M = about 43.9M chair-hours.
  • One hairdresser fills about 7 hours of chair time a day: 7 × 5.5 × 48 = 1,848 hours a year.
  • 43.9M ÷ 1,848 = about 23,700 FTEs.

Three methods, three answers between 24,000 and 27,000. You can state 25,000 to 26,000 FTEs with confidence.

Which assumption matters most

Clients per day. Barbers doing quick cuts may see 10 or more. At 10 clients a day, capacity becomes 2,640 visits a year and the answer drops to 54M ÷ 2,640 = about 20,500. Visit frequency is the second lever: at 5 visits per person instead of 6, the answer is 45M ÷ 2,112 = about 21,300. Name both and say which you would test first.

What a strong answer sounds like

"I'll size the haircuts London needs and divide by what one hairdresser can do. Men visit about seven times a year and women about five, so roughly 54 million visits. A hairdresser sees about eight clients a day, five and a half days a week, 48 weeks a year, which is about 2,100 visits. That gives roughly 26,000 full-time equivalents, or around 34,000 people if many work part time. One salon per thousand residents with three chairs each gives 27,000, so I'm comfortable with that range."

A weak answer jumps straight to "one hairdresser per 300 people, so 30,000". It might be close, but the ratio is pulled from nowhere and cannot be tested.

Common mistakes

  • Ignoring the FTE versus headcount gap. The capacity method counts full-time workloads. If the interviewer wants people, adjust for part-time work.
  • One visit length for everyone. Treating a beard trim and a full colour as the same unit distorts capacity.
  • Assuming 100% utilisation. No one is booked every minute. Eight clients a day already allows for gaps, cleaning and no-shows.

Practice

1. How many barbers (men's cuts only) work in London?

Show the answer

Men's visits: 31.5M a year. A barber does about 12 cuts a day: 12 × 5.5 × 48 = 3,168 a year. 31.5M ÷ 3,168 = about 10,000 FTE barbers.

2. What do Londoners spend on hairdressing each year?

Show the answer

Men: 31.5M visits × $30 = $945M. Women: 22.5M visits × $80 (more colour and styling) = $1.8B. Total about $2.7B a year, roughly $300 per Londoner.
